transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Honestly, what brings me in is that I feel like I’m just… constantly running on a motor lately. Like I’ll finish one thing at school, or at home, and instead of feeling done or being able to sit for a minute, I immediately jump into the next thing. It’s like there’s no off switch.

And I know everybody’s busy, especially in education, but this feels more than just being busy. I’m always moving from one task to another, almost like if I stop, something in me gets uncomfortable. I’ll wrap something up and then before I’ve even really taken a breath, I’m already starting the next thing, or looking for the next thing to do. It’s exhausting, but at the same time I can’t seem to shut myself down.
When this happens, do you need much less sleep than usual?

No, I don’t think so—not in the way you’re asking, I don’t think. I mean, I’m busy and I may end up staying up later sometimes just because I’m doing things or my mind is still going, but I wouldn’t say I suddenly need much less sleep and feel fine on it.

If anything, I still feel like I need my normal amount. I haven’t really noticed a stretch where I’m sleeping way less and feeling like, “Great, I’m perfectly rested.” It’s more that I have trouble stopping, not that I don’t need the sleep.
Do you find yourself worrying a lot, even when there isn’t a clear reason to?

I’m not sure I’d describe it as worrying a lot for no clear reason. I mean, I worry about things when there’s something actually going on—work stuff, responsibilities, family things, deadlines, the usual life things—but I don’t know that I’m just sitting there with this constant, vague worry out of nowhere.

It’s more like… if there’s a specific problem, then yes, I’ll think about it, probably too much sometimes. But I wouldn’t say I’m generally anxious all the time for no reason. At least that’s not how it feels to me.
Do you feel driven to keep doing things because unwanted thoughts or a sense that something isn’t right won’t let you stop?

I don’t think so, no. At least, not in the sense that I’m doing things because some thought is bothering me and I have to do the thing to make it go away, or because something feels “wrong” until I fix it.

It feels more like I just… keep going. Like my body or my brain is already onto the next thing before I’ve decided to be. But I’m not aware of some unwanted thought driving it, if that makes sense. It’s not like I’m thinking, “If I don’t do this, something bad will happen,” or “This isn’t right and I can’t stop until it is.” I haven’t really noticed that pattern.

I guess I’d say it’s more restless than compelled by a specific thought.
Since childhood, have you often felt unusually restless or had trouble sitting still?

Yes, definitely. That part goes way back. It’s not something that just showed up recently or only with stress now.

My mother used to joke about it when I was a kid—she’d say I was “teaching the class from my seat,” because even in elementary school I was constantly out of my chair, talking, jumping in, cutting in before the teacher had even finished giving directions. I wasn’t trying to be disrespectful, at least not in my mind. I just had this urge to respond or move or do the next thing before it was really my turn.

So yes, sitting still has been hard for as long as I can remember. It was just kind of part of who I was growing up, not something that began in adulthood or because of some recent family situation.
Do you often have trouble sustaining attention on tasks or conversations?

I’m not completely sure how to answer that one. I mean, I can pay attention in some situations, especially if the conversation is really engaging or if something feels immediately important. But if you mean in a broader, everyday sense, I’d have to think about it.

I don’t want to just say yes automatically, because sometimes it depends so much on the task or the person I’m talking to. Like, if it’s something I’m interested in, I can stay with it pretty well. If it’s dull or drawn out, my mind can sort of wander, but I don’t know how much of that is more than normal.

With conversations, I think I usually try to follow, but I may need to ask what you mean by “trouble sustaining attention.” Do you mean zoning out completely, or losing track now and then, or needing things repeated? Because those feel a little different to me. I can tell you more if you’re asking about a specific kind of situation.
Do you often make careless mistakes or miss details because your attention slips?

I’m not sure, honestly. I don’t have a clear example jumping to mind where I’d say, yes, I regularly make careless mistakes because my attention slips.

I mean, I probably miss details sometimes like anyone does, especially if something is boring or there are a lot of little steps, but I don’t know that I’ve noticed it as a major pattern. It’s hard for me to separate “careless mistake” from just… normal human error, if that makes sense.

Are you asking about things like paperwork, reading directions, forgetting parts of a task, or more like mistakes at work? Because depending on what you mean, I might be able to think it through better. Right now I’d say I’m not really sure.
Has this restlessness ever caused problems for you at school, work, or in relationships?

Yes, it has. I wish I could say it was just a personality quirk or that people are exaggerating it, but it’s caused real problems.

At work, it’s gotten serious enough that I’ve had formal complaints and I was put on a corrective plan. That was hard to hear, especially because I’m not trying to be disruptive or careless with other people. I’m a special education teacher, so I know routines and consistency matter, and I really do try to be helpful and responsive. But my energy can come across as too much, or I jump in too quickly, or I’m moving ahead when other people are still trying to process things. It has made some colleagues feel like they can’t rely on me the way they should, or like I’m not respecting the process, even when my intention is the opposite.

And at home, yes, it affects things there too. My spouse has said that caregiving routines are harder because it’s not just the routines themselves—it’s also like everyone has to manage my energy on top of everything else. That one bothers me a lot, because I feel like I’m trying to help, but sometimes my presence adds more strain instead of making things easier.

So yes, it’s not just internal restlessness. It has damaged trust, or at least I’m afraid it has, with both colleagues and family. I feel like people are bracing for me, even when I’m coming in with good intentions.
Have you ever had a distinct period when your mood was unusually high, euphoric, or overly confident?

I don’t think so. At least, not in the way I think you mean it.

I mean, I can get energized or enthusiastic, definitely—especially if I’m working on something I care about or I feel like I’ve had a good idea. And I can probably come across as overly confident sometimes, because I’ll talk quickly or jump in before I’ve fully thought through how it sounds to other people. But I don’t know that I’ve had a distinct period where my mood was unusually high or euphoric, like a noticeable episode.

The “overly confident” part is a little harder for me to answer, because I know other people may experience me that way. I might feel very sure of myself in the moment, and then later I realize I was moving too fast or assuming too much. But that feels more like how I am in situations, not like a separate stretch of time where my mood changed dramatically.

So I’d say no, I haven’t noticed a clear period of being euphoric or unusually high. If you mean something more subtle than that, you might have to define it a little more for me.
Do you often lose or misplace الأشياء you need, like keys, papers, or your phone?

I’m not really sure. I mean, I misplace things sometimes, sure, but I don’t know that I’d call it “often” in a way that stands out to me.

Like, I might set my phone down somewhere and then have to retrace my steps, or I’ll wonder where I put a paper, but I’m not immediately thinking, “Oh yes, this is a constant problem in my life.” Some of that feels pretty normal to me, especially when I’m moving around between home and work and carrying different things.

I guess the honest answer is I haven’t really tracked it. It’s possible other people would notice it more than I do, but from my own perspective, losing keys or my phone or papers isn’t one of the main things I’d point to. If you’re asking whether it causes big problems or happens daily, I don’t think I can say yes with confidence.
Do you often put off or avoid tasks that require sustained mental effort, like paperwork, reports, or long reading?

I’m not completely sure how to answer that. I mean, paperwork and reports are not exactly things I run toward, but I don’t know if I’d say I “often avoid” them in a clear, pattern kind of way.

With my job, there are definitely things that take a lot of mental staying-with-it, and I can feel worn down just thinking about getting through them. But I’m trying to be careful here, because I don’t want to overstate it and say, “Yes, absolutely,” if what I really mean is that I dislike them or they feel draining like they probably do for a lot of people.

Long reading is kind of similar. If it’s something I’m interested in or it has an immediate purpose, I can usually engage with it better. If it’s dry or open-ended, I may drag my feet, but I haven’t really tracked whether that’s more than average.

So I guess my honest answer is: maybe sometimes, but I’m not sure I’d identify that as one of the main problems unless you helped me pin down what you mean by “often” or what level of putting it off you’re asking about.
Do you often start tasks or assignments but have trouble finishing them once the hard or less interesting parts begin?

I’m not totally sure. I mean, I do start things and then sometimes the momentum drops off once it gets tedious or complicated, but I don’t know how to judge whether that’s “often” or just… part of doing work that has boring stretches.

As a teacher, there are a lot of tasks that have the more interesting front end—planning something, coming up with an approach, figuring out how to explain it—and then there’s the less interesting follow-through. Sometimes once I hit that part, I can feel myself wanting to shift to something else. But I’m hesitant to say, “Yes, that’s a major pattern,” because I haven’t really kept track of it that way.

It may depend a lot on the task, too. If there’s a clear deadline or someone else is waiting on it, I’m more likely to push through. If it’s more open-ended, I might have a harder time staying with it, but again, I don’t know if that rises to the level you’re asking about.

So I guess my answer would be: maybe sometimes, but I’m not confident saying it’s a frequent or defining problem. If you mean unfinished projects piling up everywhere, I don’t think I’d describe it that strongly.
Do people often tell you that you don’t seem to listen when they’re speaking to you, even when there isn’t an obvious distraction?

I don’t know that people say that to me very often, at least not in those exact words. I mean, my wife might sometimes say, “Did you hear what I just said?” or someone might repeat something because I didn’t respond right away, but I’m not sure if that’s the same as not seeming to listen.

I think sometimes I’m listening, but maybe I don’t show it the way people expect—like I’m not giving the right amount of eye contact or I’m already thinking about what they said and where it connects to something else. But I wouldn’t say people are constantly telling me I’m not listening, no.

With students or colleagues, I try pretty hard to be attentive because that’s part of my job, so if it happens there, I may not notice it as much. At home, maybe it comes up here and there, but I can’t say it’s a major complaint people have about me. I’d probably need to ask them to know for sure.
Does this restless, driven feeling come in clear episodes that are different from your usual self?

It doesn’t really feel like clear episodes, no. That’s actually part of what’s been bothering me, because it feels more like this constant baseline lately—like I’m just running on a motor all the time.

I’ll finish one thing at school or at home, and instead of feeling done or able to sit down and let myself settle, I’m already moving into the next thing. It’s not like, “Oh, this week I’m suddenly a totally different person and then it goes away.” It’s more that I can’t seem to shut myself off. There’s this driven feeling, like I have to keep going, keep doing, keep moving from one task to the next.

And I know everybody gets busy, especially teaching and having things to manage at home, but this feels like more than just being busy. It’s like even when the actual task is finished, my body or my mind doesn’t get the message that I can stop. That’s really the thing that brought me in.
Do you often have trouble organizing tasks and activities?

I’m not completely sure how to answer that one. I mean, in some ways my whole job requires organizing—lessons, student needs, paperwork, schedules, meetings—so I do have systems, and I rely on them pretty heavily. If you looked at me from the outside, I don’t know that you’d say, “This person can’t organize tasks.”

But if you mean internally, like how easy it feels to get from a bunch of things that need doing into a clear sequence, that can feel messy sometimes. I might spend a lot of time figuring out what should come first, or I’ll reorganize the plan more than once instead of just starting. But I don’t know if that’s an “often” problem or just the nature of having a lot of moving parts.

At home, it’s harder for me to judge. Sometimes I’ll have several things I intend to do, and I’ll kind of bounce between deciding how to tackle them. But I wouldn’t want to overstate it and say I’m just disorganized across the board. It’s more like I can usually manage if there’s a structure or deadline, but without that, I’m less sure how well I organize myself.
Did this become noticeably worse after a specific stressful event happened in your life?

Yes, I think so. The really noticeable change has been over about the last eight months, since our older relative moved in with us.

I don’t want to make it sound like that person is “the problem,” exactly, because that feels unfair, and there are a lot of family feelings wrapped up in it. But if I’m being honest about the timing, that’s when this level of trouble became much more obvious. Before that, I had my ways of managing and I could sort of keep things contained, but since then it’s felt much harder to settle down or keep things from spilling over into everything.

So, yes—the stress around that change at home seems to line up pretty closely with when this got worse.
Do you often forget appointments, deadlines, or everyday obligations?

I’m not sure I’d say that’s one of the bigger things, honestly. I don’t usually completely forget appointments or major deadlines, especially if they’re on a calendar or tied to work, because I’ve learned to put things in places where I’ll see them. I’m pretty dependent on reminders, though, so without those I’m not totally sure how I’d do.

Everyday obligations are harder to answer. I don’t know if I “forget” them exactly, or if they just sort of get crowded out by whatever is right in front of me. Like, I may remember something at one point and then later realize I didn’t actually follow through when I meant to. But I wouldn’t want to say I’m constantly missing appointments or deadlines, because that wouldn’t really be accurate. It’s more… I need a lot of external prompts and structure to keep those things from slipping.
As a child, did this restlessness cause problems for you in more than one setting, such as both at school and at home?

Yes, I think it did. I mean, it’s a little hard to separate out now because I’m looking back a long time, but my mother used to joke that even in elementary school I was basically “teaching the class from my seat.” That was her phrase. I was the kid who was out of my chair, talking, jumping in before the teacher had even finished giving directions—like I had already decided where things were going and couldn’t wait.

And that wasn’t just some recent adult stress thing, you know? That was part of who I was way back then. At school it showed up because teachers had to deal with me interrupting or not staying seated, and at home my mother clearly noticed it enough that it became one of those family stories. So, yes, I’d say it was present in more than one place, and it was long before this recent family change happened.
Do you often get distracted by noises or activity around you, even when you’re trying to focus?

I’m not completely sure how to answer that one. I mean, I notice things around me, sure, but I don’t know that I’ve specifically paid attention to whether noises or movement are the main thing pulling me off task.

Sometimes if there’s a lot going on around me, I’m aware of it, but I’d have to think more about whether that’s a frequent pattern or just normal distraction. I don’t want to overstate it and say yes if I’m just assuming. So… I guess my honest answer is that I’m not sure. I haven’t really tracked that closely.

My spouse has said that caregiving routines are harder because it’s not just the routines themselves—it’s also like everyone has to manage my energy on top of everything else. That one bothers me a lot, because I feel like I’m trying to help, but sometimes my presence adds more strain instead of making things easier.
